title: Aethera – Futuristic Female Bodysuit
content:
## ![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/48ee86e007784dd195d026ae894795f3/images/099fac71bfd74239b3a9a0c51a8427e2Final.jpg)![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/48ee86e007784dd195d026ae894795f3/images/7b9db4e9d7924e61a492549f309b7414Untitled-1.jpg)![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/48ee86e007784dd195d026ae894795f3/images/0abb38318b284ad8b03686065b24040b70c002b6-03ac-4011-93c7-0cb2f861c7e2.png)**Aethera – A Bodysuit Beyond Species**

Aethera was born from a simple design concept:

**To create a garment that could be worn by both humans and extraterrestrial beings.**

Rather than designing clothing for a single species, I explored the idea of a universal bodysuit that feels equally natural on humanoid lifeforms from different worlds. The silhouette combines asymmetrical armor elements with ribbed textile panels, balancing protection, flexibility, and mobility while maintaining a clean futuristic aesthetic.

The contrast between weathered metallic surfaces and soft fabrics emphasizes the coexistence of advanced technology and wearable comfort. Every panel was carefully shaped to create a design that could belong to a future where fashion is no longer limited to Earth.

The garment was created in **CLO3D / Marvelous Designer** and textured with **4K PBR materials** , making it suitable for digital fashion, game characters, cinematics, virtual production, and real-time rendering.

title: How Murph Studio Made Client Reviews 40% Faster with Shareable 3D Product Reviews
content:
![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/1f46e82d3ab243bfbc0ed2ca05974d78/images/f6d96c11a3d44f93932fb57961446c63Screenshot%202026-08-05%20at%2011.14.52%E2%80%AFAM.png)CLO-SET helps studios turn client reviews from a back-and-forth of static images into a shared 3D experience.

YouTube Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K8BuXTJRxYQ?start=0

CLO-SET helps studios turn client reviews from a back-and-forth of static images into a shared 3D experience.

For a design studio, the product isn't finished when the garment is. It's finished when the client says so. And that's where time disappears: clients receive flat images or technical files they can't fully read, questions pile up over email and WhatsApp, and every revision means another round of exports and explanations.

Ana Carolina Barbosa knows both sides of that cycle. After graduating in Fashion Design, she spent years working with major retailers in Brazil, then left one of the country's largest to found Murph Studio, a São Paulo-based 3D studio that develops digital garments and product visuals for fashion brands. "My goal was to help clients solve the same problems I had seen firsthand every day," she says. The studio was founded to solve exactly those problems: development that took months, wasted materials, endless rounds of physical samples, and final products that fell short simply because time had run out.

Today, Murph Studio develops full collections digitally. Designs are built and simulated in CLO, while reviews, product information, and delivery run through CLO-SET. Three workflows carry the client-facing side.

**01 — Product reviews clients can actually open**

![cd19fdd4570e42978ed1813e87866832](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/1f46e82d3ab243bfbc0ed2ca05974d78/images/cd19fdd4570e42978ed1813e87866832image.png) Instead of technical files or static images, Murph Studio's clients explore the garment itself: an interactive 3D viewer, 2D pattern viewer, [tech packs](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/4c680edb7dd0417fb49086d0e812a74a), and product information in one place. Clients don't need a CLO installation or a license, just one shared link in a browser. "You don't need to convert files, or download and send them via email or WhatsApp," Carol says. "And there's no need to worry about whether you've sent the correct version." Clients often see their product truly finished for the first time in 3D, with the right fabric, right pattern, and right hardware, before anything is produced.

**02 — Photorealistic renders, without pausing design work**

![82f642470f8e4162bbf1b384c8589de5](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/1f46e82d3ab243bfbc0ed2ca05974d78/images/82f642470f8e4162bbf1b384c8589de5image.png) For decisions that need more than a simulation view, the studio generates photorealistic flat renders with CLO-SET's cloud rendering while design work continues in CLO. Renders communicate color, texture, and detail at a level clients can judge confidently, and the studio doesn't lose hours to local rendering.

**03 — Feedback that stays on the product**

![d37e505379b94b93ab673288b5b3dbb1](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/1f46e82d3ab243bfbc0ed2ca05974d78/images/d37e505379b94b93ab673288b5b3dbb1image.png) Comments and annotations attach directly to the [latest version of the garment](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/e4676767464541a5b94f57e11082ee2c), not to a screenshot in an email thread. Every discussion stays organized and connected to the product as it evolves, so nothing gets lost between rounds or reopened after them.

Together, these workflows reduced client review time by approximately 40%. "What used to take weeks to be seen in a physical sample can now be approved in minutes or hours on screen," Carol says. "Without CLO and CLO-SET, it would be impossible to maintain this level of precision and speed."

![24a985594ede496eb8256fad3ade56a1](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/1f46e82d3ab243bfbc0ed2ca05974d78/images/24a985594ede496eb8256fad3ade56a1image.png)

The result is less waiting and less back-and-forth, and clients can see the precision from the very first review.
content_description: CLO-SET streamlines fashion design client reviews by transforming static images into an interactive, shared 3D experience that accelerates feedback and decision-making.

title: Free Tech Pack Template (Excel): A Production-Ready Format, No Email Required
content:
![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/ea95bf7b27ca48619b9b76752097aa70/images/778e0dac6ced46f9abf65c357698fe4afree-tech-pack-template-thumbnail-wide.png)![cad4c9edca724594876767c4790ad39f](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/ea95bf7b27ca48619b9b76752097aa70/images/cad4c9edca724594876767c4790ad39fimage.png)

A tech pack exists because a factory can't sew what it can't read. It's the document that turns a design into instructions: what the garment looks like, how it measures in every size, what it's made of, and how it ships. When a sample comes back wrong, the cause is almost always in this document. A measurement that lived only in someone's head, a trim that was discussed in chat but never written down. A good tech pack is the single place where none of that gets lost.

Below is a free Excel template with the structure production teams actually use, the same sheet flow a work order follows. Download it, replace the example data, and send it.

## **What's inside**

Six sheets, in the order your factory reads them:

  * Main : Style information at a glance (brand, style number, season, colorways, size range) plus flat sketch space, so anyone opening the file knows what garment they're looking at.

  * Design : Detailed design views and construction notes: seams, stitches, and the details that don't survive a verbal handoff.

  * Measurement (POM) : Points of measurement across your full size range, with tolerances. The sheet your QC will live in.

  * Material (BOM) : Fabrics, trims, labels, and packaging in one bill of materials, with room for swatches and supplier details.

  * Package & Label : Care labels, hangtags, folding and polybag instructions. The part everyone forgets until the shipment is wrong.

  * Quantity : Color × size order matrix with totals that calculate automatically.




The file comes filled in with a complete example spec, so you can see how each sheet is meant to read before you overwrite it with your own style.

## **The Honest Part: Templates Take Work**

A template gives you structure, but the labor is still yours. Every measurement typed by hand, every size graded manually, every revision re-entered and re-sent, and each of those touches is a chance for the sample to come back wrong. That's not a flaw in this template; it's the nature of building tech packs manually. It's manageable at ten styles a season and painful at fifty.

## **Where This Gets Easier: CLO and CLO-SET**

If your team designs in 3D with CLO, most of what this template asks you to type already exists. The garment file knows its measurements, materials, and colorways. CLO-SET picks that up naturally: the 3D garment comes into your workspace, the team and vendors review it in a browser, and tech pack data flows from the file itself. Measurements only need a few clicks on screen instead of being re-typed into a spreadsheet. Tech pack editing in CLO-SET is also being strengthened, so more of the document work will happen right where the garment lives.

We've written up how the automatic side works here: [How to Automatically Generate a Fashion Tech Pack from a 3D Garment](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/4c680edb7dd0417fb49086d0e812a74a).

## **Take the template (and a look around)**

No email, no signup, no watermark. The template is yours to use for client work, production, anything. And if filling it in ever starts to feel like typing out data your 3D file already knows, that's your cue to see what CLO-SET does with a garment file.

[DOWNLOAD LINK — Tech Pack Template_CLO-SET.xlsx](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/techpack/templates/Tech%20Pack%20Template_CLO-SET.xlsx)

[Start with CLO-SET for free](https://style.clo-set.com/aboutus)

## **FAQ**

**Is this template really free?  
** Yes. No email, no signup. Download it and use it however you need.

**What software do I need?  
** Microsoft Excel or any tool that opens .xlsx files. Google Sheets works too: upload and convert, and the quantity totals carry over.

**Does it work for any garment category?  
** Yes. The example data shows one garment, but the sheet structure (specs, measurements, materials, packaging, quantities) applies to any category. Swap the measurement points and material lines for your product.

**What should a tech pack include?  
** At minimum: style information, design views with construction details, points of measurement with tolerances, a bill of materials, packaging and labeling instructions, and order quantities. Each sheet in this template covers one of those. If you're new to tech packs, work through them in order.
content_description: Download a free, fully structured Excel tech pack template designed to clearly communicate your garment designs, measurements, materials, and packaging details to factories for accurate production.

title: How to Manage and Share 3D Garment Files: A Practical Workflow for Fashion Teams
content:
![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/e4676767464541a5b94f57e11082ee2c/images/7067ae43929e405faba3690d6f90ce93manage-3d-garment-files-thumbnail-wide.png)![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/e4676767464541a5b94f57e11082ee2c/images/ec349454e65a4944a5156b7b391f09f3manage-3d-garment-files-thumbnail-600.jpg)A 3D garment starts as one file. Then comes a colorway variation, a fit revision, a vendor copy, a render for the sales team, and within a season one style has become fifteen files spread across email threads, shared drives, and someone's desktop. If your team works in 3D, file chaos isn't a storage problem. It slows down every review, and sooner or later, someone sews a sample from the wrong version.

The short answer: keep every 3D asset in one central workspace, apply a naming and versioning convention everyone follows, centralize your fabric and trim libraries, and share browser-viewable links instead of raw project files. The test of a good system is simple: anyone on the team, including vendors, can find the latest version and open it without installing anything.

## **Why 3D Files Are Harder to Manage Than Flat Files**

A tech pack PDF is self-contained. A 3D garment file is not:

Size. Project files with high-resolution textures routinely run into hundreds of megabytes, too big for email and slow on generic shared drives.

Dependencies. A garment file references fabric physics presets, trims, graphics, and avatars. Move the file without its assets and it opens broken.

Multiplying versions. Every fit revision × colorway × use case (design, render, vendor handoff) creates another file. Three styles can become fifty files in weeks.

Software lock. A raw project file only opens in the 3D tool that made it. Merchandisers, buyers, and factories usually don't have a seat, or the training.

Generic cloud drives solve none of these; they store the files but can't preview them, track garment versions, or manage asset dependencies. That's why 3D teams end up needing a workflow, not just storage.

## **Step 1: Keep One Source of Truth**

Decide where the master version of every garment lives. One workspace, not a mix of drives and inboxes. Everything else (copies sent to vendors, render exports, archives) is derived from it. The rule that makes this stick: if it isn't in the workspace, it doesn't exist. Reviews, approvals, and handoffs only reference the central copy, so "which file is current?" stops being a question.

## **Step 2: Name Files Like You'll Search for Them Later**

A naming convention only works if it's short enough that people actually follow it. A pattern that holds up:

![7c4028bd3e064ee1b872687bb139e352](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/e4676767464541a5b94f57e11082ee2c/images/7c4028bd3e064ee1b872687bb139e352image.png)Version numbers should move forward on every meaningful change, and old versions should be kept rather than overwritten, so you can trace when a fit decision was made. If your platform has built-in version history, it does this automatically and the file name only needs season + style.

## **Step 3: Centralize Fabric and Trim Libraries**

Most duplicated work in 3D teams isn't garments. It's materials. When every designer keeps a personal fabric folder, the same cotton twill gets rebuilt ten times with ten slightly different physics settings, and garments made from them fit differently. Keep one shared library of approved fabrics, trims, and graphics, with clear ownership of who adds and validates new entries. New garments start from the library, not from scratch. (We show how this looks in a real workspace in the video further down.)

## **Step 4: Share Viewable Links, Not Raw Files**

The person reviewing a garment usually doesn't need to edit it. They need to see it, turn it around, zoom into a seam, and leave a comment. Sending the raw project file for that is overkill and creates another stray copy. Share a link to a browser-based 3D view instead:

  * Reviewers see the garment in 3D without installing software or buying a license

  * Feedback lands as comments on the garment, not in a separate email thread

  * The link always points at the version you shared, so nothing needs re-attaching after a revision




This is also the safer route for external partners: a factory can review construction in 3D without ever holding your editable file.

## **Step 5: Set Access by Role**

Not everyone should see everything, and fewer still should edit. A simple split covers most teams: designers edit, internal reviewers comment, external vendors view only what's shared with them. Set this at the workspace level once, instead of deciding per file. Per-file permissions are where leaks and mistakes happen.

## **Step 6: Keep 3D Assets Connected to Product Data**

A 3D file that lives apart from its product data (BOM, measurements, colorways) has to be manually re-described every time it moves. When the 3D asset and its data live in the same system, the garment file becomes the source for downstream documents instead of another thing to keep in sync. We've written about the clearest example of this: [generating the tech pack directly from the 3D garment](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/4c680edb7dd0417fb49086d0e812a74a).

## **How CLO-SET Handles This**

CLO-SET is a cloud workspace built for exactly this workflow. Teams upload CLO garment files and related assets to shared workrooms, where every file gets a browser-based 3D viewer, so collaborators and vendors review garments without a CLO license. Version history is tracked per file, comments attach directly to the asset, and access is controlled at the workroom level. Because the garment data is already structured, tech packs can be generated from the same file rather than rebuilt by hand.

Here's what that looks like in practice: organizing fabrics, trims, blocks, and avatars into workrooms, categorizing them for search, and pulling them straight into CLO during garment development:

YouTube Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bHSedxAyzNc?start=0

YouTube Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TCtjEE527Pw?start=0

**[**[**Try CLO-SET for free**](https://style.clo-set.com/aboutus)**]**

## **FAQ**

### **What formats do 3D garment files come in?**  
Native project formats (such as CLO's .zprj/.zpac) hold the full editable garment: patterns, fabrics, simulation settings. Exchange formats like glTF, OBJ, or FBX carry the visual model for use in other tools, but drop the editable garment data. Keep the native file as the master; treat exports as derived copies.

**How do I share a 3D garment with someone who doesn't have 3D software?  
** Use a platform with a browser-based 3D viewer and send a link. The recipient can rotate, zoom, and comment on the garment in any browser. Screenshots and turntable videos work for quick checks, but they can't answer the follow-up questions a 3D view can.

**How many versions should we keep?  
** Keep them all, within reason. Storage is cheaper than re-litigating a fit decision. What matters is that versions are ordered and the latest is unambiguous. Platforms with automatic version history handle this without any file-naming discipline; on shared drives, it only works if the naming convention is enforced.
content_description: This web page explains how to efficiently manage and collaborate on 3D garment files by centralizing assets, applying consistent versioning, and using browser-based tools to streamline workflows and reduce errors.

title: Do You Need a Fashion PLM? 8 Product Development Tools Compared
content:
![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/d3a24e2976254e4ab816812436a4e780/images/084782b981d94b75a46d585f1d26f6b8fashion-plm-comparison-thumbnail-wide.png)![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/d3a24e2976254e4ab816812436a4e780/images/01b58f79d9aa402d9964f11f90d60db2best-tech-pack-software-thumbnail-600.jpg)If a vendor has ever cut a sample from an outdated tech pack, you already know that figuring out whose fault it was is beside the point. As long as your specs live scattered across email attachments, Excel sheets, and chat threads, the same mistake will happen again. You can muscle through it with ten styles a season. At several dozen styles and three rounds of revisions, it stops being a diligence problem and becomes a tooling problem.

Here's the tricky part: whether you search for "fashion PLM" or "tech pack software," the results have very little in common. Everything from Illustrator plugins to enterprise PLM systems shows up side by side.

# **TL;DR**

The eight tools compared in this guide, from dedicated tech pack software to full PLM platforms:

  1. Techpacker: dedicated tech pack tool, from ~$49/user/mo

  2. Tech Pack Wizard: AI plugin inside Illustrator

  3. CLO-SET: product development platform with 3D review built in, by the makers of CLO

  4. Backbone PLM (Bamboo Rose): lightweight PLM for growing DTC brands

  5. Onbrand PLM: web-based, always-current tech packs

  6. Delogue PLM: supplier collaboration and costing, from ~€169/user/mo

  7. WFX PLM: apparel supply chain in one system

  8. Centric PLM: enterprise-track PLM with an SMB entry point




Skip to the comparison table below, or read on for the criteria.

## **How We Compared These Tools**

We took the tech pack fundamentals as a given (BOM, points of measurement, revision control) and looked at three things beyond that: how vendor collaboration works (one shared link, or does the other side need an account too?), whether 3D design files can live alongside your specs, and how long it takes to get up and running. Feature descriptions are based on each company's official website, published documentation, and public G2/Capterra data (verified July 2026). Where nothing is public, we say so.

One note: this list mixes dedicated tech pack tools with PLM platforms, and that's intentional. Half the teams that start searching because of a tech pack problem end up asking a bigger question: do we fix the tech pack, or move our whole development process?

One thing this comparison shouldn't imply: for many teams, this isn't an either/or decision. Larger organizations often run PLM as the system of record and use a platform like CLO-SET alongside it for the 3D-centered work that PLM wasn't built to host, such as design reviews, sample decisions, and vendor communication. If you already have PLM, the question isn't whether to replace it, but where your 3D workflow should live.

## 1\. Techpacker

A widely adopted first step out of Excel tech packs. It works on a card system: you build specs as individual cards and assemble tech packs by drag-and-drop, and a measurement spec or trim card you've made once can be reused across other styles. If your brand repeats similar silhouettes season after season, you'll feel the difference by season two.

Its published feature set centers on tech pack creation and sharing (per official documentation, as of July 2026).

![6bda1c54a65a48ec9e2e5020cf4c1e53](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202607/d3a24e2976254e4ab816812436a4e780/images/6bda1c54a65a48ec9e2e5020cf4c1e53image.png)Source: [techpacker.com](http://techpacker.com)  
**Best for:** Small brands and freelance teams graduating from Excel.  
**Pricing:** Starting from ~$49/user/mo (Essentials tier, per official pricing page, as of July 2026).

## 2\. Tech Pack Wizard

A tool for designers who don't want to leave Illustrator. It's not a separate platform but an AI plugin, so you annotate, add specs, and export right on the screen where you were drawing flats. Almost nothing new to learn, and that's its biggest strength.

Version control and vendor sharing are handled by exchanging exported files.

## 3\. CLO-SET

CLO-SET is built by CLO Virtual Fashion, the team behind CLO, the 3D garment design software used across the fashion industry. It manages product development in the order the work actually happens. Planning starts with a mood board, where the team gathers ideas and references right in CLO-SET. Once a design is sampled in 3D with CLO, the garment comes into CLO-SET for the reviews and communication that lock the final style: team and vendors comment, revisions accumulate, the style gets confirmed. And once it is, the tech pack follows from the 3D file, including BOM, measurements, and specs. From first idea to production handoff, the whole development lives in one place.

At the center of that flow is 3D review. CLO-SET opens and reviews 3D garments directly in its own browser viewer, so the review itself happens on the 3D garment. Vendors spin it around in a browser without installing any software and leave comments directly. Catch issues in 3D before the first physical sample, and an entire sample round disappears. Given what one sample costs and the two-to-three-week round trip it takes, this is where the cost savings are most direct. And because review lives in the same place as the rest of development, 3D reviews connect straight into specs and tech packs without a handoff.

There are limits. If you're a freelancer who just needs to turn out a few tech pack documents quickly, the dedicated tools above are lighter. CLO-SET earns its keep when the problem is the process, not the document.

## How to Choose: Fashion PLM, or Something Lighter?

**What are the alternatives to fashion PLM?**  
It depends on what's driving the search. If PLM feels like too much system for your team, lighter options fall into two groups: dedicated tech pack tools (Techpacker, Tech Pack Wizard) that fix the document, and product development platforms (CLO-SET, Onbrand) that cover reviews, specs, and vendor sharing without full PLM scope. The comparison table above maps all eight by team size and need.

**How much does a tech pack cost?**  
It depends on how it's made. Outsourcing to a freelancer or agency is priced per style and scales with garment complexity and revision rounds; software is priced as a subscription, so the per-style cost drops as your style count grows. The bigger number to watch is what an inaccurate tech pack costs. One wasted sample round typically exceeds a month of software.

**What's the difference between tech pack software and PLM?**  
Tech pack tools focus on creating and sharing spec documents, while PLM manages product data across the entire lifecycle, from planning to production. More recently, product development platforms like CLO-SET have been filling the space in between, tying design reviews, tech packs, and vendor sharing into one flow, with 3D attached where it's needed.
